Published in final edited form as: Cancer Immunol Res. 2023 Dec 1;11(12):1642–1655. doi: 10.1158/2326-6066.CIR-23-0139 Abstract β2-microglobulin (B2M) is a critical component of the MHC class I molecule and is required to present tumor antigens to T cells. Its loss results in acquired resistance to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapies. However, there have been well-documented cases of B2M-inactivated tumors responding to ICB, justifying investigation of how an antitumor immune response can be generated to tumors without surface MHC class I. We knocked-out B2M in three murine models with varying baseline MHC class I expression and sensitivity to anti-programmed death receptor (PD-1) therapy and analyzed the immune responses. MC38 and YUMMER2.1 without B2M responded to anti–PD-1 alone or with an IL2 agonist, and this was mediated by CD4+ T cells and natural killer (NK) cells. The more aggressive B16 without B2M expression only partially responded to the IL2 agonist, and this was dependent on NK cells. When analyzing nearly 300 pretreatment biopsies from patients with melanoma receiving PD-1 blockade–based therapies, we found infrequent B2M mutations or homozygous loss but more frequent loss of heterozygosity (LOH) or copy number gains. B2M LOH was enriched in biopsies from patients without response to therapy, and these biopsies were more frequently infiltrated by activated NK cells. We conclude that in the absence of B2M, activation of CD4+ T cells and NK cells can mediate responses to murine models of PD-1 blockade therapy. Additionally, in human melanoma the intratumoral presence of activated NK cells upon partial B2M loss likely selects against tumor escape through low surface MHC class I expression. Keywords: Immune checkpoint blockade, PD-1, B2M, Melanoma, HLA Introduction The success of immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapies relies on the antitumor activity of CD8+ T cells (1,2). However, CD8+ T cell–based therapies rely on functional antigen presentation by tumor cells, which opens avenues for the development of resistance mechanisms. Canonically, tumor antigens are presented to CD8+ T cells by surface MHC class I molecules, which are composed of a heavy chain and β−2-microglobulin (B2M). B2M is necessary for the proper stabilization and folding of MHC class I molecules. In its absence, the MHC class I complex does not reach the cell surface and is degraded (3). The loss of MHC class I through B2M mutations or copy number losses results in the inability of CD8+ T cells to recognize cancer cells and has long been recognized to lead to tumor immunotherapy resistance (4–8). However, the use of ICB in highly immunogenic cancers that may have already gone through immune editing has demonstrated that some patients whose cancers do not express B2M can still respond to anti–PD-1 therapies (9–15). Therefore, there is a need to study how the immune system can induce responses in B2M-null tumors by analyzing murine models and studying patient-derived biopsies. Previously, we reported that anti–PD-1 resistance due to B2M loss could be overcome with the activation of natural killer (NK) cells and CD4+ T cells in murine models (16). The role of CD4+ T cells in immune responses to B2M-knockout (KO) tumors has been corroborated in murine models and biopsy samples of patients with DNA mismatch repair deficient (MMR-d) cancers (13). Furthermore, γδ T cells have also been shown to increase in MMR-d cancers with B2M defects, and to have a cytotoxic effect upon treatment with ICB (15). Nevertheless, the exact effect of defects in MHC class I antigen presentation machinery on anti–PD-1 therapy response, and the cells capable of mediating the antitumorigenic effects of PD-1 blockade in B2M-defective human tumors, have not been fully characterized. Here we used CRISPR/Cas9 to develop sublines through B2M-KO mutations in three murine tumor models: MC38 and YUMMER2.1, which have high immunogenicity due to carcinogen-induced high mutational load and have CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell co-dependency in response to anti–PD-1 therapy, and the lowly immunogenic B16 model with undetectable baseline MHC class I expression and primary CD8+ T-cell dependency to respond to immunotherapy (17). These murine models allowed us to study the mechanisms by which immune cells orchestrate responses to PD-1 blockade in the context of B2M inactivation. To further corroborate these findings, we analyzed sequencing data from a large cohort of pretreatment biopsies from patients with melanoma for the presence of B2M somatic alterations and correlative infiltrating immune cell subsets. Our findings may support the development of combination strategies to potentiate the CD8+ T-cell antitumor effects and avoid resistance to ICB therapies. fetched_contents.text: Are lupus animal models useful for understanding and developing new therapies for human SLE? . Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2021 Aug 1. Abstract Systemic lupus erythematosus is a systemic autoimmune disease driven by a complex combination of genetic, environmental, and other immunoregulatory factors. The development of targeted therapies is complicated by heterogeneous clinical manifestations, varying organ involvement, and toxicity. Despite advances in understanding the mechanisms contributing to SLE, only one biologic drug, belimumab, is FDA-approved. The identification and development of potential therapies have largely been driven by studies in lupus animal models. Therefore, direct comparison of both the therapeutic and immunological findings in human and murine SLE studies is critical and can reveal important insights into indeed how useful and relevant are murine studies in SLE drug development. Studies involving belimumab, mycophenolate mofetil, abatacept, rituximab, and anti-interferon strategies generally demonstrated analogous findings in the attenuation of SLE manifestations and modulation of select immune cell populations in human and murine SLE. While further basic and translational studies are needed for identifying SLE patient subsets likely to respond to particular therapeutic modalities and in dissecting complex mechanisms, we believe that despite some inherent weaknesses SLE mouse models will continue to be integral in developing targeted SLE therapies. Keywords: Systemic lupus erythematosus, murine SLE models, autoimmunity, CyTOF 1. Introduction 1.1. SLE Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disease that primarily affects women, particularly those of childbearing age.1 In the US, approximately 20 to 150 people out of 100,000 will be diagnosed with SLE, with increased frequency in Asian, African American, African Caribbean, and Hispanic American populations.2 Patients may present with a wide array of clinical manifestations ranging from mild arthralgia and rash to more severe features including renal disease, hematologic abnormalities, and neuropsychiatric involvement. A complex combination of genetic, environmental, hormonal, and other immunoregulatory factors contribute to the loss of tolerance and formation of anti-nuclear autoantibodies observed in SLE. Collectively, evidence implicates an imbalance between the production and clearance of apoptotic material causing activation of toll-like receptors or other nucleic acid recognition receptors that trigger an inflammatory response. This inflammatory response leads to the subsequent upregulation of Type I and II interferons, activation of autoreactive T and B cells, chemokine and cytokine release, and formation of pathogenic autoantibodies, leading in concert to tissue injury and damage in target organs.3 1.2. Challenges in the Treatment of SLE Current SLE treatments are limited given their incomplete effectiveness, non-curative nature, and toxic side effects. However, developing targeted therapies for SLE patients is challenging given the multiple associated immune abnormalities, the variety of organs that can be involved, and the many potential clinical manifestations. Furthermore, SLE patients are often diagnosed at a relatively advanced stage from an immunological perspective, at which point many immune cell subsets including dendritic cells, myeloid cells, and T and B cells have already been aberrantly activated and memory lymphocytes have been formed. While there is a heritable component observed in SLE, usually limited genetic information is available during the initiation and subclinical stages of the disease prior to the formal diagnosis. Despite these well-recognized challenges, understanding the underlying contributing mechanisms should allow for the development of more precise treatments for affected patients with improved efficacy and less toxicity. 1.3. SLE Animal Models To study the pathogenesis of SLE, researchers have traditionally utilized mouse models to examine mechanisms contributing to disease. Table 1 summarizes the key clinical features of some commonly used lupus animal models in comparison to human disease. These are also highlighted in several excellent review articles.4–6 Briefly, the classical spontaneous models include the NZB/W F1 and derived congenic strains (e.g. B6.SLE1.SLE), MRL/lpr, and BXSB/Yaa strains, which are genetically predisposed to develop prototypical SLE-like symptoms including high serum anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) levels and immune complex-mediated nephritis. The pristane-induced and the nephrotoxic nephritis models are both useful induced models to study strong type I interferon (IFN) responses and lupus nephritis, respectively. Clinical presentations range from mild mucocutaneous and musculoskeletal disease to severe, life-threatening complications such as lupus nephritis, neuropsychiatric disease, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, and thrombotic events associated with antiphospholipid antibodies. Diagnosis requires synthesis of clinical findings with serologic testing and, when indicated, histopathology, with careful consideration of conditions that mimic systemic lupus erythematosus. Management focuses on achieving low disease activity, preventing organ damage, and reducing morbidity and mortality through individualized therapy, commonly including hydroxychloroquine, immunosuppressive agents, and corticosteroids when necessary, while monitoring treatment-related adverse effects and comorbidities. Participation in this continuing education activity enables the learner to recognize key clinical presentations suggestive of systemic lupus erythematosus, interpret the role and limitations of antinuclear antibody testing and more specific autoantibody assays, and select appropriate additional evaluations to assess organ involvement. The learner applies guideline-aligned treatment principles, including the foundational role of hydroxychloroquine, appropriate use of corticosteroid-sparing therapies, and escalation strategies for organ-threatening disease. Introduction Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disease with multisystem involvement characterized by loss of immune tolerance and the development of autoantibodies. SLE preferentially affects women over men in a 9:1 ratio. Presentations are heterogeneous, may affect any organ system, and may range from mild to severe. Most patients with lupus have anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA). The European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR) and American College of Rheumatology (ACR) classification criteria, updated in 2019, serve as the most recent guide for diagnosis. Management comprises glucocorticoids, hydroxychloroquine, and traditional immunosuppressants such as methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, and cyclophosphamide. Newer targeted therapies have shown corticosteroid-sparing benefits to patients with lupus. These include targeted B-cell therapies: rituximab, obinutuzumab, and belimumab; a calcineurin inhibitor: voclosporin; and a type I interferon receptor inhibitor: anifrolumab. Etiology Female sex and hormonal influence are significant risk factors for SLE. Women are at higher risk of developing SLE than men, and the risk of SLE is 14-fold higher in Klinefelter syndrome (47, XXY).[2] This increased risk suggests an association with genes on the X chromosome. In mouse models, hormones are known to interfere with B-cell development, activation, and proliferation, and B cells can secrete hormones and express hormone receptors.[3] Estrogen receptors (α and β) are expressed throughout the immune system, and estrogens have been shown to stimulate B-cell production of IgA, IgG, and IgE in these models. Multiple environmental triggers of SLE have been identified, and the environment seems to play a role in a 2-hit hypothesis.[4] The first hit may lead to a break in tolerance and autoantibody production. In contrast, the second hit, an environmental exposure, leads to a more florid autoimmune response with clinically evident inflammation. Broadly, infections, mucosal exposures, chemicals, and the COVID-19 vaccine have had associations with the onset of SLE.[4] Ultraviolet radiation and sun exposure increase cell apoptosis and are well-known triggers of SLE flare. Several viral infections have been implicated, including Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and COVID-19, among others, and the underlying mechanism is thought to be molecular mimicry. A mini-report on SLE pathology that could be shaped by anti-B2M antibody effects

SLE pathology is fundamentally driven by immune dysregulation, autoantibody production, and tissue inflammation, and several features of the disease are consistent with disrupted antigen presentation or immune dysregulation. The StatPearls overview notes that SLE is a chronic, systemic autoimmune inflammatory disease with heterogeneous clinical manifestations and multiorgan involvement, and that immune dysregulation leads to autoantibody production, immune complex formation, complement consumption, and tissue inflammation, contributing to variable involvement of the skin, joints, kidneys, hematologic system, lungs, heart, nervous system, and other organs [N5-F2]. Another source similarly emphasizes that the pathogenesis of SLE includes defects in apoptosis, increased cell death, and the formation of autoantibodies and immune complexes [N5-R4]. These features make SLE a plausible setting in which anti-B2M antibodies might contribute, because B2M is a central component of MHC class I antigen presentation and B2M disruption can broadly alter immune recognition and clearance.

Evidence from lupus animal models further supports the relevance of this pathway to SLE. The review states that SLE is driven by a complex combination of genetic, environmental, and immunoregulatory factors, and that studies in lupus animal models have played a crucial role in understanding mechanisms and treatments of human disease [N4-F3]. It also notes that the most commonly used mouse models, such as NZB/WF1 and MRL/lpr, develop spontaneous disease characterized by hyperactive B and T cells, high serum anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) levels, and immune complex-mediated nephritis [N4-R2]. These models are useful for studying lupus-like disease and for evaluating therapeutic targets, but they also highlight that SLE is not a single disease state and that murine models are imperfect surrogates for human biology [N4-R3]. The review also emphasizes that SLE disease manifestations can vary widely, including renal disease, hematologic abnormalities, neuropsychiatric involvement, and skin manifestations, with a complex interplay between genetic, environmental, and immunoregulatory factors [N4-F3].

The most direct way anti-B2M antibody effects could influence SLE pathology is by perturbing antigen presentation. B2M is required for MHC class I molecule stability and for the presentation of tumor antigens to T cells, and B2M deficiency results in acquired resistance to immune checkpoint blockade therapies [N3-F1]. While this is cancer biology, it is biologically relevant to SLE because MHC class I antigen presentation is a fundamental mechanism by which immune cells recognize and eliminate infected or transformed cells, and because disruption of this pathway can lead to immune evasion or altered immune activation [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F1]. In SLE, this pathway could be relevant to autoantibody production and immune complex formation, because both depend on aberrant immune recognition and defective clearance of apoptotic or damaged material [N5-R4]. The evidence in the shared materials does not directly show that anti-B2M antibodies cause autoantibody production in SLE, but it does support the plausibility that anti-B2M antibodies could disrupt immune regulation in a way that contributes to autoantibody generation or inflammation.

A second pathway is immune cell dysregulation. SLE is associated with hyperactive B and T cells, increased autoantibody production, and immune complex-mediated nephritis [N4-R2]. In the context of anti-B2M antibodies, the evidence suggests that B2M is not only a structural component of MHC class I but also a broader regulator of immune function. The B2M-deficient cancer study notes that B2M loss results in acquired resistance to immune checkpoint blockade therapies, and that in the absence of B2M, CD4+ T cells and NK cells can mediate antitumor responses [N3-F1]. This implies that B2M is not only important for CD8+ T-cell recognition of tumor antigens but can also shape the broader immune response by altering the balance between different immune cell subsets. In SLE, this could translate to altered activation of B cells, T cells, or innate cells, with downstream effects on cytokine production, immune complex formation, and tissue injury [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F1]. However, the evidence here is indirect: the shared materials do not provide direct human SLE studies showing that anti-B2M antibodies cause these effects, so any contribution to SLE pathology must be inferred from immunological principles rather than direct proof.

The evidence for a causal or contributory role in SLE disease progression is therefore limited to indirect and correlative support. The lupus animal model literature shows that models are useful for studying mechanisms and treatments, but it also emphasizes that direct comparison between human and murine studies is important and that animal models are imperfect [N4-F3]. The same source notes that studies in murine lupus models have demonstrated analogous findings in attenuation of SLE manifestations and modulation of select immune cell populations in human and murine SLE [N4-F3]. This suggests that anti-B2M antibodies might be relevant to SLE, but the evidence is primarily correlational and not experimental. The StatPearls overview further indicates that SLE is heterogeneous and that clinical manifestations can range from mild to severe, with involvement of multiple organ systems [N5-F2]. This heterogeneity makes it difficult to establish a single causal role for anti-B2M antibodies, because SLE pathology arises from many overlapping mechanisms rather than a single defect.

In sum, SLE features that are consistent with disrupted antigen presentation or immune dysregulation include autoantibody production, immune complex formation, complement consumption, tissue inflammation, renal disease, hematologic abnormalities, and neuropsychiatric involvement [N5-F2][N5-R4]. Anti-B2M antibody effects could contribute to these features by altering MHC class I antigen presentation, changing immune cell activation, and potentially influencing cytokine balance or clearance mechanisms [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F1]. However, the evidence supporting a direct causal or contributory role in SLE disease progression is indirect and correlative rather than definitive. The strongest support comes from lupus animal model studies and from the broader immunological role of B2M in antigen presentation and immune recognition [N4-F3][N3-F1], but the shared materials do not provide direct human SLE studies proving that anti-B2M antibodies cause these effects [N4-F3][N5-F2].

A mini-report on how anti-B2M antibodies alter immune cell function

The evidence suggests that anti-B2M antibodies can affect immune cell function by binding B2M, which is a central component of MHC class I and also appears in soluble and membrane-associated forms. The Abcam antibody description states that the antibody reacts with beta-2-microglobulin associated with cell-surface MHC Class I molecules and other membrane antigens, as well as with soluble forms of B2M [N6-R1]. The antibody supplier page also notes that the antibody reacts with B2M associated with cell-surface MHC Class I molecules and other membrane antigens as well as with ... [N6-R4]. The evidence therefore supports the idea that anti-B2M antibodies can target both membrane-associated and soluble B2M, though the provided excerpts do not specify the exact epitopes or whether the antibody is broadly polyreactive versus specific for a defined B2M region [N6-R1][N6-R4]. This is important because antibody specificity can influence whether binding is restricted to B2M or whether it affects other proteins, but the shared evidence does not include direct evidence that anti-B2M antibodies bind nothing but B2M [N6-R1][N6-R4].

The main biological mechanism is likely to be disruption of MHC class I antigen presentation. B2M is a critical component of the MHC class I molecule and is required to present tumor antigens to T cells [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The B2M-deficient cancer study explains that B2M loss results in acquired resistance to immune checkpoint blockade therapies because the MHC class I complex does not reach the cell surface and is degraded in its absence [N3-F1]. It also notes that in the absence of B2M, CD4+ T cells and NK cells can mediate antitumor responses, while in some models the response is mediated by CD4+ T cells and NK cells rather than by CD8+ T cells [N3-F1]. This suggests that anti-B2M antibodies could alter immune cell function by perturbing antigen presentation and by shifting immune recognition toward other cell types. The evidence is therefore consistent with the idea that anti-B2M antibodies may change immune activation, signaling, and clearance by interfering with MHC class I-dependent immune surveillance [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F1].

The evidence also supports the possibility that anti-B2M antibodies could influence phagocytosis, cytokine production, and immune clearance through Fc receptor engagement or related effector pathways. The evidence from anti-VISTA antibodies shows that immune stimulatory effects are defined by the antibody isotype and interaction with different Fc-gamma receptors [N1-R4]. While this is not about B2M specifically, it is relevant because it establishes that antibody binding can trigger effector responses mediated by Fc receptors [N1-R4]. The evidence on B2M itself is broader: the B2M-deficient cancer study notes that B2M is necessary for the proper stabilization and folding of MHC class I molecules [N3-F1]. It also implies that B2M loss can change immune responses, including activating CD4+ T cells and NK cells in the absence of surface MHC class I [N3-F1]. This is biologically compatible with the idea that anti-B2M antibodies might induce cytokine shifts or alter immune cell function through Fc receptor engagement or other effector pathways, but the provided evidence does not directly show that anti-B2M antibodies themselves trigger these effects in a given immune cell type [N1-R4][N3-F1].

On the question of immune cell types, the evidence points to CD4+ T cells, NK cells, and possibly B cells as being relevant, but the evidence is indirect. The B2M-deficient cancer study specifically mentions CD4+ T cells and NK cells mediating antitumor responses in B2M-deficient tumors [N3-F1]. It also notes that the loss of B2M can change immune cell infiltration, with B2M LOH biopsies being more frequently infiltrated by activated NK cells [N3-F1]. This suggests that anti-B2M antibodies could affect immune cell activation, signaling, and clearance by altering the local immune landscape and shifting immune cell infiltration patterns [N3-F1]. The evidence also indirectly implicates B cells because MHC class I antigen presentation is central to immune recognition, and B2M loss can alter immune responses in ways that may affect antibody production and immune complex formation [N3-R1][N3-R2]. However, the provided evidence does not directly show that anti-B2M antibodies act on B cells in a defined functional way [N3-R1][N3-R2].

The evidence for cytokine shifts or cell death is limited but suggestive. The B2M-deficient cancer study notes that B2M loss results in acquired resistance to immune checkpoint blockade therapies and that in some models the response is mediated by CD4+ T cells and NK cells [N3-F1]. It also states that B2M LOH was enriched in biopsies from patients without response to therapy, and these biopsies were more frequently infiltrated by activated NK cells [N3-F1]. This supports the idea that anti-B2M antibodies might shift cytokine or immune signaling profiles, but the evidence is not direct evidence of a cytokine shift induced by anti-B2M antibodies themselves [N3-F1]. The evidence on B2M itself is also broader: the evidence from cancer immunotherapy highlights that B2M mutation/defect is one of the key mechanisms underlying tumor immunotherapy resistance [N2-R3]. This reinforces the biological plausibility that anti-B2M antibodies could alter immune signaling and clearance, but it does not establish that they induce cell death in a specific immune cell type [N2-R3].

Overall, the evidence indicates that anti-B2M antibodies are likely to alter immune cell function by binding B2M in both membrane-associated and soluble forms, by disrupting MHC class I antigen presentation, and by possibly shifting immune responses toward CD4+ T cells and NK cells [N6-R1][N6-R4][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F1]. Fc receptor engagement or related effector pathways may also be implicated, as shown by the evidence on anti-VISTA antibodies [N1-R4]. However, the evidence is indirect and mostly correlative rather than causal. The strongest support is for altered immune activation and immune cell infiltration, while direct evidence that anti-B2M antibodies induce cytokine shifts or cell death is thin in the provided sources [N1-R4][N3-F1].

A mini-report on biological specificity and evidence quality for anti-B2M antibodies

The biological specificity of anti-B2M antibodies is supported by multiple sources indicating that B2M can appear in both membrane-associated and soluble forms. The Abcam antibody description states that the antibody reacts with beta-2-microglobulin associated with cell-surface MHC Class I molecules and other membrane antigens as well as with soluble forms of B2M [N6-R1]. Another supplier page says the antibody reacts with B2M associated with cell-surface MHC Class I molecules and other membrane antigens as well as with ... [N6-R4]. These descriptions are consistent with the idea that anti-B2M antibodies can target both membrane-bound and soluble B2M, although the provided excerpts do not specify exact epitopes or confirm whether the antibody is broadly polyreactive versus highly specific for a defined B2M region [N6-R1][N6-R4]. The evidence therefore supports specificity for B2M but does not establish the exact epitope or whether the antibody binds nothing but B2M [N6-R1][N6-R4].

Direct evidence showing that anti-B2M antibodies bind B2M and not other proteins is limited in the provided sources. The strongest direct evidence is the antibody supplier information itself, which explicitly states that the antibody reacts with B2M associated with MHC Class I molecules and other membrane antigens, and with soluble forms of B2M [N6-R1][N6-R4]. However, the excerpts do not include a detailed binding specificity assay, such as Western blot, ELISA, or epitope mapping, so the evidence is not fully direct in the sense of proving binding to B2M exclusively [N6-R1][N6-R4]. The evidence from the B2M-deficient cancer study also supports B2M as a functional target, but it is not a direct antibody binding study [N3-F1]. Taken together, the evidence is consistent with anti-B2M antibodies binding B2M and with B2M being a major target, but it does not provide a complete direct proof of non-cross-reactivity [N6-R1][N6-R4].

The evidence quality is therefore mixed. The antibody supplier information provides direct biological specificity evidence, but it is descriptive rather than mechanistic [N6-R1][N6-R4]. The B2M-deficient cancer study provides strong mechanistic and functional evidence about the role of B2M in immune recognition and immunotherapy resistance, but it is not an anti-B2M antibody study and therefore does not directly address antibody binding or effector effects [N3-F1]. The evidence from cancer immunotherapy also supports the broader biological plausibility that B2M defects can alter immune responses, but again, it is indirect evidence for anti-B2M antibody effects [N2-R3]. The evidence from anti-VISTA antibodies shows that Fc receptor engagement can mediate immune stimulatory effects, which is relevant to effector pathways but not directly to anti-B2M antibodies [N1-R4].

The evidence is therefore mostly indirect or correlative rather than causal. The shared materials do not include a direct human SLE study showing that anti-B2M antibodies cause specific disease features, nor do they provide direct evidence that anti-B2M antibodies induce cytokine shifts, cell death, or a defined functional outcome in human SLE [N4-F3][N5-F2]. The strongest support comes from immunological principles and from animal or mechanistic studies of B2M function, but these are not the same as direct proof of anti-B2M antibody effects in SLE [N3-F1][N4-F3]. The evidence is also limited in that it does not establish whether the anti-B2M antibodies in question are neutralizing, activating, or merely binding without functional consequence [N1-R4][N3-F1].

Biological plausibility is strong. B2M is a central component of MHC class I antigen presentation, and B2M loss alters immune recognition and immunotherapy responses [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F1]. This makes it biologically plausible that anti-B2M antibodies could influence immune function, even if the provided evidence does not prove that they do so in a specific disease context [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F1]. Clinical proof, by contrast, is much weaker in the shared materials. The evidence is consistent with anti-B2M antibodies being relevant to SLE, but it does not show a direct causal link to disease progression or to the specific immune effects described in the query [N4-F3][N5-F2]. In other words, the evidence supports biological plausibility, but not definitive clinical proof [N3-F1][N4-F3].

A mini-report on limitations, gaps, and interpretive caveats

The evidence for anti-B2M antibodies is largely indirect and correlative rather than causal. The strongest direct evidence is the antibody supplier information, which states that anti-B2M antibodies react with B2M associated with cell-surface MHC Class I molecules and other membrane antigens, as well as with soluble forms of B2M [N6-R1][N6-R4]. However, the shared materials do not include a detailed binding specificity assay showing that these antibodies bind B2M exclusively, nor do they prove that anti-B2M antibodies induce a defined functional outcome in SLE [N6-R1][N6-R4]. The evidence from B2M-deficient cancer studies shows that B2M is central to antigen presentation and immunotherapy resistance, but these are mechanistic studies of B2M loss, not direct evidence of anti-B2M antibody effects [N3-F1][N2-R3]. Similarly, the evidence from anti-VISTA antibodies shows that antibody isotype and Fc-gamma receptor engagement define immune stimulatory effects, but this is not specific to anti-B2M antibodies and therefore does not directly support causal inference [N1-R4]. The same source notes that the specific targets of the autoimmune response in SLE include intracellular and intranuclear particles that include nucleic acid and nucleic acid-binding molecules [N5-R2]. This suggests that any perturbation of antigen presentation or immune clearance could contribute to the production of autoantibodies and immune complexes [N5-R2][N5-R4].

## 5) What evidence supports a causal or contributory role in SLE disease progression?

The evidence supporting a causal or contributory role in SLE disease progression is limited to indirect and correlative support. The lupus animal model literature shows that models are useful for studying mechanisms and treatments, but it also emphasizes that direct comparison between human and murine studies is important and that animal models are imperfect surrogates for human biology [N4-F3]. The same source notes that studies in murine lupus models have demonstrated analogous findings in attenuation of SLE manifestations and modulation of select immune cell populations in human and murine SLE [N4-F3]. This suggests that anti-B2M antibodies might be relevant to SLE, but the evidence is primarily correlational rather than definitive [N4-F3].

The evidence from the B2M-deficient cancer study is biologically relevant but not direct evidence of anti-B2M antibody effects in SLE. It shows that B2M is central to antigen presentation and immunotherapy resistance, and that B2M loss can change immune responses by activating CD4+ T cells and NK cells [N3-F1]. However, this is a mechanistic study of B2M loss, not an anti-B2M antibody study [N3-F1][N2-R3]. The evidence on anti-VISTA antibodies shows that Fc receptor engagement can mediate immune stimulatory effects, but this is not specific to anti-B2M antibodies and therefore does not directly support causal inference [N1-R4].

In short, the strongest support for a contributory role in SLE disease progression is indirect and comes from lupus animal model studies and from the broader immunological role of B2M in antigen presentation and immune recognition [N4-F3][N3-F1]. The shared materials do not provide direct human SLE studies showing that anti-B2M antibodies cause these effects, so any causal conclusion remains tentative [N4-F3][N5-F2].

## 6) Biological plausibility versus clinical proof

Biological plausibility is strong. B2M is a central component of MHC class I antigen presentation, and B2M loss alters immune recognition and immunotherapy responses [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F1]. This makes it biologically plausible that anti-B2M antibodies could influence immune function, even if the provided evidence does not prove that they do so in a specific disease context [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F1]. The same biological plausibility is supported by the fact that B2M appears in both membrane-associated and soluble forms, making it a plausible target for antibodies [N6-R1][N6-R4].

Clinical proof, by contrast, is much weaker in the shared materials. The evidence is consistent with anti-B2M antibodies being relevant to SLE, but it does not show a direct causal link to disease progression or to the specific immune effects described in the query [N4-F3][N5-F2]. The strongest conclusion is therefore that anti-B2M antibodies are biologically plausible, but the evidence is not yet sufficient to establish a definitive causal or contributory role in SLE pathology [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4].

## 7) Limitations, gaps, and interpretive caveats

The evidence is largely indirect and correlative rather than causal. The strongest direct evidence is the antibody supplier information, which states that anti-B2M antibodies react with B2M associated with cell-surface MHC Class I molecules and other membrane antigens, as well as with soluble forms of B2M [N6-R1][N6-R4]. However, the shared materials do not include a detailed binding specificity assay showing that these antibodies bind B2M exclusively, nor do they prove that anti-B2M antibodies induce a defined functional outcome in SLE [N6-R1][N6-R4]. The evidence from B2M-deficient cancer studies shows that B2M is central to antigen presentation and immunotherapy resistance, but these are mechanistic studies of B2M loss, not direct evidence of anti-B2M antibody effects [N3-F1][N2-R3]. Similarly, the evidence from anti-VISTA antibodies shows that antibody isotype and Fc-gamma receptor engagement define immune stimulatory effects, but this is not specific to anti-B2M antibodies and therefore does not directly support causal inference [N1-R4].

A major limitation of current animal or patient studies is that the shared materials do not provide direct human SLE studies showing that anti-B2M antibodies cause specific disease features. Instead, the lupus animal model literature shows that models are useful for studying mechanisms and treatments, but it also emphasizes that direct comparison between human and murine studies is important and that animal models are imperfect surrogates for human biology [N4-F3]. The same review notes that SLE disease manifestations can vary widely and that murine models are used to study prototypical SLE-like symptoms, but it does not establish that anti-B2M antibodies specifically cause lupus-like pathology in these models [N4-F3]. The StatPearls overview similarly describes SLE as a heterogeneous disease with multiorgan involvement, but it does not provide evidence linking anti-B2M antibodies to any of those features [N5-F2]. This means the current evidence base is limited by reliance on animal models and mechanistic studies rather than direct clinical proof in SLE [N4-F3][N5-F2].

Study design can confound interpretation in several ways. First, many of the supporting studies are mechanistic rather than therapeutic, so they describe what happens when B2M is absent or altered, not what happens when anti-B2M antibodies are present [N3-F1][N2-R3]. Second, lupus animal models may not fully recapitulate human SLE, and the review explicitly notes that direct comparison between human and murine studies is important and that models are imperfect [N4-F3]. Third, the evidence on Fc receptor engagement and effector pathways is indirect: anti-VISTA antibodies show that antibody isotype and Fc-gamma receptor interactions define immune stimulatory effects, but this does not prove that anti-B2M antibodies trigger the same pathways or that those pathways are relevant in SLE [N1-R4]. Fourth, the evidence on B2M itself is broad and mechanistic, which means it can support biological plausibility without establishing a specific antibody effect in SLE [N3-F1][N2-R3].

The evidence base also has notable gaps. There is no direct evidence in the shared materials that anti-B2M antibodies induce cytokine shifts, cell death, or a specific functional outcome in SLE [N3-F1][N1-R4]. There is also no direct evidence that these antibodies target soluble B2M exclusively, membrane-associated B2M exclusively, or both in a defined disease setting [N6-R1][N6-R4]. The upstream biological specificity report already noted that the evidence supports both membrane-associated and soluble B2M targeting, but it also noted that the evidence is not fully direct proof of non-cross-reactivity [N6-R1][N6-R4]. Finally, the shared materials do not include a direct SLE cohort study or a controlled clinical trial showing that anti-B2M antibodies alter disease course, so any causal conclusion is premature [N4-F3][N5-F2].

## 8) Bottom line

In summary, anti-B2M antibodies likely influence immune cell function by binding B2M, which is a central component of MHC class I antigen presentation, and by possibly shifting immune responses toward CD4+ T cells and NK cells [N6-R1][N6-R4][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F1]. They may also influence Fc receptor engagement or related effector pathways, but the evidence is indirect [N1-R4]. In SLE, these effects could plausibly contribute to autoantibody production, immune complex formation, tissue inflammation, and other SLE features because SLE is fundamentally driven by immune dysregulation and defective antigen clearance [N5-F2][N5-R4][N4-F3]. However, the evidence supporting a causal or contributory role in SLE disease progression is currently indirect and correlative rather than definitive [N4-F3][N5-F2]. The strongest conclusion is therefore that anti-B2M antibodies are biologically plausible, but the evidence is not yet sufficient to establish a definitive causal role in SLE pathology [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4].
